trial_name.text: Study 104 and Study 111 (pooled), in treatment-naive adults

citations.quote: The primary safety assessment of GENVOYA was based on Week 48 pooled data from 1733 subjects in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trials, Study 104 and Study 111, in antiretroviral treatment-naïve HIV-1 infected adult subjects.
Phase 3 trials 292-0104 and 292-0111 and phase 2 trial 292-0102 compared (E/C/F/TAF) to Stribild (Elvitegravir/Cobicistat/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate, STB) in treatment naïve adults.

citations.quote: The primary safety assessment of GENVOYA was based on Week 48 pooled data from 1733 subjects in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trials, Study 104 and Study 111, in antiretroviral treatment-naïve HIV-1 infected adult subjects.

endpoint.text: Proportion of subjects with HIV-1 RNA < 50 copies/mL at Week 48 (snapshot analysis)

citations.quote: Pooled Virologic Outcomes of Randomized Treatment in Studies 104 and 111 at Week 48a in Treatment-Naïve Subjects
d. HIV-1 RNA less than 50 copies per mL.

The primary safety assessment of GENVOYA was based on Week 48 pooled data from 1733 subjects in two randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trials, Study 104 and Study 111, in antiretroviral treatment-naïve HIV-1 infected adult subjects.

In both Study 104 and Study 111, subjects were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either GENVOYA (N=866) once daily or STRIBILD (elvitegravir 150 mg, cobicistat 150 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, TDF 300 mg) (N=867) once daily.

result.text: HIV-1 RNA < 50 copies/mL at Week 48: 92% GENVOYA vs 90% STRIBILD; treatment difference 2.0% (95% CI: -0.7% to 4.7%), establishing non-inferiority

trial_name.text: Study 109, in virologically-suppressed adults switched to GENVOYA

citations.quote: In Study 109, the efficacy and safety of switching from either ATRIPLA, TRUVADA plus atazanavir (given with either cobicistat or ritonavir), or STRIBILD to GENVOYA once daily were evaluated in a randomized, open-label trial of virologically-suppressed (HIV-1 RNA less than 50 copies per mL) HIV-1 infected adults (1196 of 1436 enrolled and treated were evaluable for efficacy).
Phase 3 trial 292-0109 was a switch trial in which adults who were visibly suppressed on STB were randomized to either switch to (E/C/F/TAF) or continue their successful STB regimen.

In Study 109, the efficacy and safety of switching from either ATRIPLA, TRUVADA plus atazanavir (given with either cobicistat or ritonavir), or STRIBILD to GENVOYA once daily were evaluated in a randomized, open-label trial of virologically-suppressed (HIV-1 RNA less than 50 copies per mL) HIV-1 infected adults (1196 of 1436 enrolled and treated were evaluable for efficacy).

result.text: At Week 48, 96% of patients who switched to GENVOYA had HIV-1 RNA < 50 copies/mL compared to 93% of patients who remained on baseline regimen

citations.quote: In the switch study 109, in virologically suppressed patients, 96% of patients who switched to Genvoya after 6 months on a stable regimen had HIV-1 RNA < 50 copies per mL compared to 93% of patients who remained on their baseline antiretroviral regimen.

indication.text: Indicated as a complete regimen for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older who have no antiretroviral treatment history or to replace the current antiretroviral regimen in those who are virologically-suppressed (HIV-1 RNA less than 50 copies per mL) on a stable regimen for at least 6 months

citations.quote: GENVOYA is a four-drug combination of elvitegravir, an HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), cobicistat, a CYP3A inhibitor, and emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), both HIV-1 nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and is indicated as a complete regimen for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older who have no antiretroviral treatment history or to replace the current antiretroviral regimen in those who are virologically-suppressed (HIV-1 RNA less than 50 copies per mL) on a stable antiretroviral regimen for at least 6 months with no history of treatment failure and no known substitutions associated with resistance to the individual components of GENVOYA. key_safety.text: Most common adverse reaction (incidence >= 10%) is nausea (10% GENVOYA vs 13% STRIBILD); other common reactions include diarrhea (7% vs 9%), headache (6% vs 5%) and fatigue (5% vs 4%). Serious warnings include new onset or worsening renal impairment and bone loss/mineralization defects.

citations.quote: Most common adverse reaction (incidence greater than or equal to 10%, all grades) is nausea. (6.1)

- New onset or worsening renal impairment: Assess creatinine clearance, urine glucose, and urine protein in all patients before initiating GENVOYA therapy and monitor during therapy. Monitor serum phosphorus in patients with chronic kidney disease. (5.7)
- Bone loss and mineralization defects: Consider monitoring BMD in patients with a history of pathologic fracture or other risk factors of osteoporosis or bone loss. (5.8)

detail.text: Lactic acidosis/severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (including fatal cases) reported with nucleoside analogs, and post-treatment severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B in patients coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV who discontinue emtricitabine and/or tenofovir products; GENVOYA is not approved for treatment of chronic HBV

citations.quote: Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with the use of nucleoside analogs in combination with other antiretrovirals [see *Warnings and Precautions* (5.1)].

Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who are coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV and have discontinued products containing emtricitabine and/or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and may occur with GENVOYA.

Genvoya contains three previously approved drugs and one new molecular entity: elvitegravir (EVG), an HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor; coabistat (COBI), a CYP 3A inhibitor; emtricitabine (FTC), a nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitor, in addition to the new tenofovir (TFV) prodrug, tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF).
